stem: A claims-triage step keeps a human reviewer because its outcome, loss ratio, surfaces in 12 months. Override rate is the readiness proxy; it rose from 4% to 11% this month. The director cites this proof and asks to remove review. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Reject the request: a rising override rate signals growing disagreement, not growing trust; investigate before automating further.
Approve removing review: the rising rate proves reviewers trust the model enough to intervene less.
Automate the step outright; it is high-volume and machine-readable, which already justifies full automation.
Replace the human reviewers with a more capable model, since fewer overrides would follow from better outputs.

whyRight: Override rate is a proxy for reliability; a rate that rose from 4% to 11% means reviewers are overriding more often, which is evidence against readiness, not for it. The director's reading inverts what the metric measures.

whyWrong.B: The stem states the rate rose, meaning reviewers intervened more often, the opposite of growing trust; reading a rising rate as proof of confidence inverts the evidence.
whyWrong.C: High volume and machine-readability are fit signals, but the section also requires correctness to be visible immediately; a rising override rate says it currently is not.
whyWrong.D: Swapping in a more capable model does not diagnose why disagreement is rising; it discards the review step's signal instead of investigating the cause behind it.

t1Clause: rose from 4% to 11% this month
lessonKey: automating before disagreement further growing investigate override rate reject request rising signals trust

stem: A moderation pipeline outputs a JSON verdict with a confidence score for an automated router. A human panel now reviews cases below that threshold, and the chair says reviewers can't tell why a case was flagged. What should the pipeline send to the panel instead?

opts.t: Reasoning and citations alongside the verdict, since the panel is the consumer and must weigh the case.
The same JSON verdict and confidence score the router already receives, unchanged.
A full transcript of every intermediate reasoning step plus the raw input document, unfiltered.
The existing confidence score, with a stricter threshold so fewer cases reach the panel.

whyRight: The output consumer determines the shape of the contract; a human panel weighing borderline cases needs the reasoning and citations behind a verdict, not just the score already built for the automated router's routing decision.

whyWrong.B: The confidence score alone is what already reaches the panel; it is the reason reviewers cannot tell why a case was flagged, not a fix for it.
whyWrong.C: A full unfiltered transcript replaces a designed, shape-matched contract with a raw dump the panel must now parse itself, which is worse for a time-pressed reviewer, not better.
whyWrong.D: Raising the threshold changes which cases reach the panel; it does nothing about the output shape those cases arrive in, which is the stated complaint.

t1Clause: A human panel now reviews cases below that threshold
lessonKey: alongside citations include reasoning verdict

stem: An invoice-intake pipeline processes 100,000 documents a day. 96% arrive in one standard layout; 4% use formats the team hasn't catalogued yet, and those often need a step no prior document required. Which architecture should the team implement?

opts.t: An agent for every document, since it can adapt to any format without hardcoded rules.
A fixed workflow for the standard layout, routing anything unmatched to an agentic exception path.
A fixed workflow for the standard layout, sending anything unmatched to a human queue.
A single retrieval-augmented call that looks up the correct layout template before extracting fields.

whyRight: Matching each population to its cheapest rung serves both correctly: a fixed workflow handles the enumerable 96% at the lowest cost and highest testability, while the agentic exception route absorbs the 4% whose paths cannot be listed in advance.

whyWrong.A: An agent for every document pays nondeterminism and token cost on the 96% whose format is already known, to serve a requirement only the remaining 4% actually has.
whyWrong.C: A human queue handles the unmatched 4% but drops the stated requirement that those cases still need automated processing through some path, not a manual dead end.
whyWrong.D: Retrieval solves a missing-data lookup problem; it does not solve routing a request down an enumerable path versus an unlistable one, which is what the 4% requires.

t1Clause: 96% arrive in one standard layout; 4% use formats the team hasn't catalogued yet
lessonKey: agentic exception route workflow

stem: A coordinator already passes synthesis findings downstream as structured content-plus-metadata records, preserving source, document, and page for a regulated audit trail. A senior reviewer asks for a cleaner prose-only summary without the metadata block, calling it easier to read. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Keep the structured handoff as-is; a prose-only summary would remove the metadata the audit trail requires.
Treat this as a coverage gap: have the coordinator re-delegate targeted queries and re-invoke synthesis before responding.
Replace the structured handoff with the prose summary, and add a separate compliance review step to catch citation errors.
Replace the structured handoff with the prose summary the reviewer requested, since readability is the stated concern.

whyRight: The structured content-plus-metadata handoff already satisfies the citation and audit-trail requirement; a prose-only summary flattens content and provenance together, which is exactly the failure the passing format exists to prevent, regardless of how the request is framed.

whyWrong.B: Coverage gaps are a synthesis-completeness problem solved by re-delegating queries; this request is about output format and citation integrity, a different failure the coordinator did not cause.
whyWrong.C: A compliance review step can catch a citation error after the fact, but it does not restore the per-claim metadata the prose summary already discarded at synthesis.
whyWrong.D: Readability is the reviewer's stated preference, not the compliance requirement the handoff format exists to satisfy; the audit trail needs the metadata regardless of how the summary reads.

t1Clause: preserving source, document, and page for a regulated audit trail
lessonKey: audit handoff keep metadata only prose remove requires structured summary trail would

stem: A compliance-reporting pipeline splits into nine agent calls, one per data field, each seeing only the prior call's single output. The compliance officer reports increasingly conflicting figures across fields. A senior architect proposes splitting further, one call per field per source. Select two corrections.

opts.t: Merge steps back toward the point where each unit again shares the context that made figures consistent.
Stop splitting once each unit has one evaluation criterion and one failure mode, not a fixed field count.
Split further into one call per field per source, since finer granularity has historically improved reliability.
Keep the nine-call structure and add a final pass that reconciles conflicting figures across all outputs.

whyRight: The nine-way split has passed its stopping rule: units no longer share context, and conflicting figures are the direct symptom. Restoring shared context by merging, then re-splitting only where one evaluation criterion and one failure mode genuinely require it, fixes the cause rather than compensating downstream.

whyWrong.C: Splitting further multiplies handoffs and repeats the context loss already causing conflicts; the historical pattern cited does not hold once units share less, not more.
whyWrong.D: A reconciliation pass detects conflicting figures after they occur; it does not restore the shared context the split removed, so the same conflicts recur at the next report.

t1Clause: splits into nine agent calls, one per data field

stem: A workflow must meet a 3-second p95 latency commitment and hold cost down at 50,000 requests a day. It runs five serial steps including enrichment, and routes every case through the same full-size model regardless of difficulty. Select two independent fixes.

opts.t: Parallelize the independent steps only, leaving the enrichment step inside the request path untouched.
Keep the current serial chain unchanged, and add caching plus a monitoring alert for SLA breaches.
Move the enrichment step off the request path by precomputing it at ingest time.
Route by confidence tier and use the smallest model that clears the accuracy bar for routine cases.

whyRight: The SLA fails on serial depth; cost is driven by routing every case through a full-size model. Moving enrichment off the request path removes the SLA-breaking step, and confidence-tier routing with the smallest sufficient model removes the cost driver.

whyWrong.A: Parallelizing alone still leaves enrichment inside the request path, so the tail latency the commitment is written against keeps breaching; it also does nothing for cost.
whyWrong.B: Caching and an alert instrument the breach the serial chain keeps producing rather than removing its cause, and neither action lowers the per-request model cost.

t1Clause: must meet a 3-second p95 latency commitment
lessonKey: bar clears confidence enrichment ingest model move off path per plus precompute request routing smallest tier

stem: A VP sponsoring a drafting tool for renewal letters plans to judge success from user feedback after launch, without recording current handling time or turnaround days for the 40,000 letters processed yearly. What should the architect do first?

opts.t: Build the drafting tool now and gather user feedback after launch to see whether it helped.
Deploy the tool with usage dashboards and derive the baseline retrospectively from those logs.
Measure current handling time and turnaround days for renewal letters before committing to a design.
Skip baseline measurement and frame the rollout as a transformation success story instead.

whyRight: Turnaround and handling time are the units the business case will be judged in; without a recorded before, the launch cannot be shown to have helped even if it works, which is the exact failure the misconception invites.

whyWrong.A: Waiting for after-launch feedback captures no before figure; the improvement claim has nothing recorded to compare against.
whyWrong.B: Deployed system logs reconstruct downstream a measurement the pre-project step could have captured cleanly beforehand.
whyWrong.D: Renewal-letter drafting already exists as a human task, so an efficiency baseline applies; transformation framing is for capabilities that did not exist before.

t1Clause: for the 40,000 letters processed yearly (an already-existing, human-done process)

stem: A support system's citations became inaccurate after last week's document refresh; compliance relies on them for a regulated audit trail across 30,000 monthly tickets. Model version and prompt are unchanged. Which fix should the architect apply?

opts.t: Re-index and refresh the retrieval layer's embeddings so lookups reflect the newly published source documents.
Replace the underlying model with a more capable one, since it is the newest available version.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to double-check each citation before responding.
Capture the mismatched citations and route them into the evaluation set for future model tuning.

whyRight: The citations broke immediately after the document refresh while the model and prompt held steady, which locates the fault in the retrieval layer; re-indexing against the refreshed sources fixes the cause instead of the model or the prompt.

whyWrong.B: The model version did not change, so the model is not the failure point; replacing it does not touch the stale retrieval index causing the mismatch.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction asks the model to try harder; it cannot correct citations pointing at documents the index has not updated to reflect.
whyWrong.D: Model version and prompt are stated as unchanged, so this is not a tuning problem; routing it to the eval set delays the fix without touching the index.

t1Clause: the citations went wrong immediately after a scheduled document refresh
lessonKey: indexing layer retrieval route signal

stem: A vendor-onboarding pipeline runs the same five checks for every submission across 2,000 vendors monthly, but one step reconciles an uploaded document set whose count, order, and naming vary unpredictably per vendor. How should that step be designed?

opts.t: Keep the other four checks fixed; give the reconciliation step an agent planning its approach per submission.
Extend the fixed pipeline's reconciliation logic to cover the most common document layouts seen so far.
Replace the entire five-check pipeline with one agent planning every step for each submission.
Route any submission with more than three documents to a human reviewer instead.

whyRight: Four of the five checks are enumerable and belong in a fixed pipeline, but the reconciliation step's shape is genuinely unlistable per vendor; giving only that step an agent buys adaptive planning where it is actually needed, and nowhere else.

whyWrong.B: Extending the template to the most common layouts covers the majority silently, but drops the vendors whose document sets do not match any listed shape.
whyWrong.C: The other four checks are enumerable and fixed by requirement; replacing them with agentic planning buys nondeterminism the stated task never asked for.
whyWrong.D: Sending the variable cases to a human reviewer abandons the automation requirement for exactly the population that needed a working design.

t1Clause: whose count, order, and naming vary unpredictably per vendor
lessonKey: agent approach checks fixed four give keep other per planning reconciliation step submission

stem: An expense agent extracts a vendor name from each receipt, and a downstream step needs that name to look up the approved spending category, across 50,000 monthly submissions with a 24-hour reimbursement commitment. How should the steps be orchestrated?

opts.t: Keep both steps in the current order but switch to a faster underlying model to shorten wall-clock time.
Dispatch both steps together from a single coordinator turn, since that is how independent subtasks are parallelized.
Chain the steps sequentially so the lookup runs only after extraction returns the vendor name.
Let both steps run as issued and add a monitoring check flagging any lookup with an empty vendor name.

whyRight: The lookup step cannot begin until it has the vendor name the extraction step produces, which is a real data dependency; sequential chaining is required, and issuing both in one turn would send an empty value downstream.

whyWrong.A: A faster model shortens each call but does not remove the dependency; the lookup still cannot run before extraction has returned a name.
whyWrong.B: Single-turn dispatch parallelizes independent subtasks; here the lookup depends on the extraction's output, so issuing both together sends the lookup an empty value.
whyWrong.D: Monitoring an empty vendor name after the call detects the failure but does not prevent it; the sequencing itself must guarantee the value exists first.

t1Clause: a downstream step needs that name to look up the approved spending category

stem: A claims-intake team must meet a stated six-hour acknowledgment SLA and hold cost per claim within a set ceiling as intake volume triples during renewal season. Which architecture should the team adopt?

opts.t: Route every claim through confidence-tier logic to the smallest model that clears the bar, minimizing cost per claim.
Keep the current pipeline and add an automated alert that escalates whenever the acknowledgment SLA is breached.
Parallelize the independent intake checks to meet the SLA, applying confidence-tier routing only to hold cost within the ceiling.
Replace the pipeline with a fully autonomous agent that decides each claim's routing case by case.

whyRight: The SLA is a stated commitment that filters designs before comparison; parallelizing removes the serial depth causing the miss, and confidence-tier routing keeps cost inside the ceiling. The pure cost-tier design meets cost alone and still breaches the commitment, which is the trap this facet targets.

whyWrong.A: Confidence-tier routing to the smallest model lowers average cost, but it does nothing about the serial depth causing the SLA miss under peak volume.
whyWrong.B: An alert on a breach reports the failure after it happens; it does not remove the serial dependency that causes the SLA to be missed.
whyWrong.D: A case-by-case agent's cost is a distribution, not a point; its tail can breach both the cost ceiling and the acknowledgment SLA under tripled volume.

t1Clause: must meet a stated six-hour acknowledgment SLA
lessonKey: commitment meeting one pick

stem: A bank's compliance pipeline classifies 10,000 transaction alerts per day into risk tiers under a 2-second latency budget, and drafts the referral letter language sent to a named regulator whenever a tier triggers escalation. Which model strategy should be used?

opts.t: Use the smallest, fastest model for every step, since the volume and latency budget dominate the task.
Route bulk classification to the fast model, but reserve a higher-capability model for drafting the regulator referral text.
Run the entire pipeline, including bulk classification, on the highest-capability model available, to be safe.
Fine-tune the fast model on past referral letters instead of testing whether a stronger base model suffices.

whyRight: The volume and latency budget fit the fast model for bulk classification, but the referral text requires open-ended judgment when addressing a regulator — a rung the fast model's own accuracy bar wasn't built to clear, so that step alone needs the higher-capability model.

whyWrong.A: Volume and latency alone would justify this for pure classification, but the stem's own escalation requirement is an open-ended judgment call this model can't reliably clear.
whyWrong.C: Upgrading bulk classification too adds cost and latency the 2-second budget doesn't have room for, when only the escalation step needs the extra capability.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning is the expensive lever; it doesn't test whether a stronger base model already handles regulator-facing drafting without any additional training.

t1Clause: drafts the referral letter language sent to a named regulator whenever a tier triggers escalation
lessonKey: bulk but capability classification drafting fast higher model referral regulator reserve route text

stem: A subscription service's support-agent system prompt refuses any discussion of account cancellation, correctly blocking retention-abuse requests. A consumer-protection rule now requires the same agent to process cancellations within 48 hours when requested through a dedicated retention tool, with legal sign-off. What should change?

opts.t: Add the exception into the system prompt's top-level guardrail language, so it applies to every tool.
Add a scoped exception to the retention tool's own system prompt, leaving the blanket guardrail in place elsewhere.
Move the cancellation check into client-side validation before requests ever reach the model.
Document the new exception in team onboarding materials, without changing the system prompt itself.

whyRight: The blanket guardrail still correctly blocks retention abuse elsewhere, so it should stay; the legitimate need is scoped to one tool, and guardrails belong at the layer where the exception actually applies — a per-tool addition, not a blanket rewrite.

whyWrong.A: The need is scoped to one tool; rewriting the top-level guardrail applies the exception everywhere, undoing protection the guardrail still correctly provides elsewhere.
whyWrong.C: A client-side check never reaches the model itself — the same failure as setting a behavioral rule through an environment variable.
whyWrong.D: Documentation elsewhere in the pipeline never reaches the model as an instruction, so its behavior toward cancellation requests won't change.

t1Clause: when requested through a dedicated retention tool
lessonKey: add blanket elsewhere exception guardrail leaving own place prompt retention s scoped system tool

stem: A multi-step reconciliation agent compares entries across 12 ledgers using a step-by-step reasoning cue; a prior test without the cue produced a higher error rate. A product manager proposes dropping the cue now, since responses already return within budget. What should happen?

opts.t: Keep the reasoning cue; the prior test already showed accuracy drops on this task without it.
Drop the cue now that latency is within budget, since token savings outweigh a one-time test result.
Replace the reasoning cue with a bounded scratchpad to cut tokens while preserving most of the accuracy benefit.
Remove the cue, since the task's format looks similar to previous single-step tasks that didn't need one.

whyRight: The task is genuinely multi-step, and the cue is already verified necessary: removing it earlier measurably raised the error rate. Nothing in the stem states a latency conflict, so the sophisticated-sounding token-saving proposal would reopen the accuracy failure the cue was added to prevent.

whyWrong.B: The prior test already measured a higher error rate without the cue; token savings don't outweigh evidence the stem itself provides.
whyWrong.C: This targets a latency conflict the stem never states exists; the plain cue already works without needing to be bounded.
whyWrong.D: The task compares entries across 12 ledgers in multiple steps; treating it as single-step misreads its actual shape.

t1Clause: since responses already return within budget
lessonKey: accuracy already cue drops keep prior reasoning showed task test without

stem: An HR assistant answers thousands of daily employee queries from a 40-page benefits handbook containing about 30 scattered bullet facts, none more critical than another, and keeps missing facts buried in the middle of the document. What should be changed?

opts.t: Leave the document's structure unchanged, since it's well under the model's effective context window.
Pull the single most business-critical fact into a highlighted block near the top of the handbook.
Convert the scattered bullets into explicit headed sections grouped by topic, even without one dominant fact.
Shorten the handbook to a strict length limit before employee queries reach the model.

whyRight: No single fact in the handbook is more critical than another, so the fix is structural, not a top-of-document highlight built for one dominant fact. Headed sections grouped by topic restore retrievability across the whole middle, which a 40-page scattered-bullet document actually needs.

whyWrong.A: A 40-page handbook queried thousands of times a day is exactly the scale the effect occurs at; 'short input' doesn't describe this document.
whyWrong.B: The stem states no fact is more critical than another, so highlighting a single fact targets a problem this handbook doesn't have.
whyWrong.D: Shortening under a length limit risks cutting exactly the scattered facts that are already going missing.

t1Clause: none more critical than another
lessonKey: convert even explicit findings first grouped headed one sections summary topic without

stem: A legal team requires a compliance disclaimer that reflects today's date to appear first in a high-volume, latency-sensitive support prompt built on a large, byte-identical cached prefix. Which placement satisfies the compliance requirement without invalidating the cache?

opts.t: Insert the disclaimer ahead of the cached prefix, as the literal first bytes of the prompt.
Keep the prefix ordering unchanged, adding the disclaimer as the next block after it.
Split the static prefix around the disclaimer so it sits mid-block, preserving partial reuse of the surrounding text.
Disable caching for this prompt and regenerate the full prefix with the disclaimer prepended on every call.

whyRight: The compliance requirement is about the disclaimer's presence and prominence, not its literal byte position. Keeping the static prefix first and adding the disclaimer immediately after it preserves the byte-identical cache while still surfacing the disclaimer at the very start of the response.

whyWrong.A: Treats 'first' as a literal byte-position requirement rather than the compliance team's actual intent, and inserting dynamic content ahead of the prefix invalidates the entire cache.
whyWrong.C: Splitting the prefix around the disclaimer breaks the single stable prefix caching depends on, so the surrounding text is no longer byte-identical across calls.
whyWrong.D: Discards a working cost and latency lever the workload doesn't need to give up, when the compliance need is satisfiable without disabling caching at all.

t1Clause: the prompt is high-volume, latency-sensitive
lessonKey: adding after block disclaimer keep next ordering prefix unchanged

stem: A contract-review pipeline runs 200 calls a day on a mid-tier model. One step needs deep reasoning over ambiguous, high-stakes clauses, and latency isn't a stated limit there. What is the lowest-cost change that meets the requirement without over-provisioning the rest of the pipeline?

opts.t: Enable extended thinking only for the ambiguous-clause step, leaving the rest of the pipeline on the current model.
Move the entire pipeline to a larger, more capable model to raise reasoning quality everywhere.
Add a strict token budget to the ambiguous step to control cost, without changing how it reasons.
Fine-tune the current model on past contract decisions before touching this step's reasoning approach.

whyRight: Extended thinking is the lightest lever that reaches the reasoning depth the ambiguous step needs, leaving the other 200 daily calls on their current, cheaper model. Upgrading the entire pipeline reaches for a far more expensive rung the stated requirement never calls for.

whyWrong.B: Upgrading the entire pipeline raises capability everywhere the requirement doesn't call for it, adding cost and latency to 200 daily calls to fix a bottleneck in one step.
whyWrong.C: A token budget controls spend but does nothing for reasoning quality on an ambiguous, high-stakes step — the bottleneck is depth, not tokens.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning requires curating training data and a retraining cycle before it touches this step's reasoning, an expensive detour around a same-day fix.

t1Clause: the reasoning gap is isolated to one step in the pipeline rather than spread across most of the workload
lessonKey: enable extended larger model moving rather step than thinking whole workload

stem: A support bot's tool-routing prompt has six few-shot examples, all drawn from the most common, easily-routed requests, yet still misroutes high-value escalation requests weekly, flagged by the support-ops lead. Applying the principle that examples must target the failure distribution, which change is correct?

opts.t: Add three or four examples demonstrating the exact required response format for escalation replies.
Add a post-processing classifier that flags likely misroutes for a human reviewer to catch after the fact.
Keep the six examples as they are and add a default-tool fallback for any ambiguous escalation request.
Replace the six examples with new ones drawn from the actual misrouted escalation cases.

whyRight: Few-shot examples teach by pattern-matching to what they show; examples drawn from easy, common cases don't resemble the ambiguous escalation requests actually failing. Replacing them with examples from the observed failure distribution targets exactly the pattern the prompt is missing, regardless of how many examples existed before.

whyWrong.A: This targets output-formatting precision, a real fix for inconsistent formatting, but the stated failure is misrouting to the wrong tool, not inconsistent response format.
whyWrong.B: A classifier that flags likely misroutes for a human catches failures after they happen instead of fixing the routing prompt itself.
whyWrong.C: A generic fallback for ambiguous requests contradicts the stated fact that these are high-value escalations needing correct, specific routing.

t1Clause: the bot misroutes ambiguous escalation requests to the wrong tool
lessonKey: distribution drawn examples failure observed replace them

stem: A coding-assistant session runs hundreds of turns. An early instruction — never modify files under one protected directory — must hold for the rest of the session, while older turns are summarized to control token cost. Which design satisfies both?

opts.t: Let the rule live inside the rolling summary along with everything else from early turns.
Pin the never-modify-this-directory rule in a persistent structured block, re-included every call, kept separate from the rolling summary.
Stop summarizing altogether and resend the full unabridged history every call to guarantee nothing is lost.
Move the protected-directory rule into the system prompt once, then drop it from every later call to save tokens.

whyRight: Pinning the rule into a stable structured block that sits outside the rolling summary guarantees it is resent unchanged every call, while the rest of the conversation still gets summarized to control token growth. A rule that must never change needs a slot summarization never touches.

whyWrong.A: Repeated re-summarization passes can paraphrase or drop the rule over hundreds of turns, risking exactly the drift a never-change requirement cannot tolerate.
whyWrong.C: Resending the full unabridged history defeats the stated goal of controlling token cost as the conversation grows, an unneeded trade for a single pinned fact.
whyWrong.D: Dropping the rule from later calls assumes the API remembers it between requests, but nothing sent in an earlier call persists unless it is resent.

t1Clause: the early decision must hold unchanged for the rest of the session
lessonKey: block call decision every included into persistent pin re rolling separate structured summary

stem: A returns-processing agent holds five role-scoped tools used in one refund decision: lookup, return-window check, fraud flag, refund issuance, and credit application. Ahead of peak volume, a reviewer proposes splitting it into eligibility and execution agents for Finance. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Split into eligibility and execution agents, adding a shared correlation ID so both calls trace to one refund request.
Split into a role-scoped eligibility agent and a role-scoped execution agent, as the reviewer proposes.
Remove the fraud-flag tool so the agent holds four tools instead of five, avoiding the need to split at all.
Keep the tools in one agent; splitting would separate return-window check from refund issuance, risking stale eligibility.

whyRight: The five tools already form a small, single-role decision set — exactly the range scoping is meant to produce, not the oversized, multi-role sprawl the split remedy targets. Splitting a set this size doesn't shrink any decision space; it only adds an unneeded coordination hop between agents.

whyWrong.A: A shared correlation ID makes the split traceable, but traceability doesn't answer whether splitting was needed — it wasn't, since five tools were never an oversized decision space.
whyWrong.B: This is the answer for an oversized, multi-role tool surface; splitting a genuinely small, single-decision set of five tools adds a hop this scenario never needed.
whyWrong.C: Fraud review is a needed capability the workflow uses, not the cause of the split proposal; removing it sidesteps the question instead of answering it.

t1Clause: the agent already holds only five role-scoped tools used together in one refund decision
lessonKey: agent check eligibility issuance keep one refund return risking separate splitting stale tools window would

stem: An agent's toolset includes a bulk-export capability no current workflow calls. Security proposes logging every export call and reviewing it monthly, calling this least privilege in practice, ahead of a regulator's access-minimization audit next quarter. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Remove the bulk-export capability from the tool set; no workflow needs it, so logging only compensates.
Keep the capability, and log every export call for the regulator's review.
Keep the capability, but restrict export calls to a limited weekly time window.
Keep the capability, but require a manager's confirmation before each export call.

whyRight: Least privilege means the permission does not exist, not that it exists under watch. Since no workflow calls bulk-export, removing it closes the gap outright; logging, time-boxing, and confirmation are controls for privileges the team has actively decided to keep, which this one is not.

whyWrong.B: Logging records that the export happened after the fact; it never stops an unneeded capability from being used, and the regulator wants access minimized, not narrated.
whyWrong.C: A time window narrows when the unneeded export can run, not whether it should exist at all, leaving the capability available every week.
whyWrong.D: Manager confirmation gates a use the workflow was never meant to have; a legitimate need is what confirmation is for, and this capability has none.

t1Clause: no current workflow calls the bulk-export capability

stem: A support-triage system sits at its 3-second p95 SLA with no slack, three accuracy points short of target. Static preamble is resent uncached on every call, and a redundant retrieval hop duplicates one lookup. A reranking pass would add 300ms. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Add the reranking pass and quietly extend the SLA to 3.3 seconds without consulting the business.
Cut the number of retrieved chunks to make room for the reranking pass inside budget.
Add the reranking pass now, and monitor p95 latency weekly to catch any SLA breach.
Fix the caching and the redundant hop first; only then decide whether the reranking pass fits inside the recovered budget.

whyRight: No slack exists, so any added stage risks the SLA outright. The uncached preamble and the duplicate hop are wasted latency already in the pipeline; recovering that budget through restructuring costs no accuracy, unlike cutting context or breaching the SLA for a reranking pass.

whyWrong.A: Extending the SLA without the business's sign-off breaches a stated commitment to buy accuracy nobody authorized, at a system already out of slack.
whyWrong.B: Cutting retrieved context removes a working mechanism and typically loses more accuracy than the reranking pass would return, the opposite of the goal.
whyWrong.C: Weekly monitoring reports a breach after it happens; it does not stop the reranking pass from pushing an already zero-slack system over budget.

t1Clause: no slack exists in the latency budget
lessonKey: before caching context cutting hops latency look ordering redundant retrieved wasted

stem: Per policy, an observability system inherits the sensitivity of what it captures. A clinical-support agent's tracing plan logs full patient records to a store every engineer can query, deferring redaction and retention ahead of a compliance audit. What should the architect require?

opts.t: Encrypt the trace store at rest and require engineers to sign in through single sign-on.
Add per-stage timing to the tracing plan, and ship the store without other changes.
Design redaction, retention limits, and access control for the trace store now, alongside the tracing pipeline itself.
Pause tracing entirely until legal signs off on a full data-handling policy for the store.

whyRight: The trace store now holds full patient records, so it inherits their sensitivity the moment it exists. Redaction, retention limits and access control belong on the pipeline's launch date, not a later phase, because deferring them leaves regulated data exposed to every engineer with query access.

whyWrong.A: Encryption and single sign-on protect the store from outside attackers but do nothing about every engineer's standing entitlement to query patient records inside it.
whyWrong.B: Per-stage timing helps diagnose a latency regression, not a data-sensitivity gap; patient records still sit in a store with no redaction or scoped access.
whyWrong.D: Pausing tracing removes a working diagnostic capability the team needs, rather than scoping the store's sensitivity the way the principle actually requires.

t1Clause: the tracing plan logs full patient records, i.e. the traces will contain regulated content
lessonKey: access control design pipeline redaction retention same store time trace

stem: A helpdesk knowledge base holds support threads of 3 to 40 messages, chunked message by message across 50,000 tickets a month. Retrieved chunks are often a lone reply with no problem statement, missing a 2-minute response SLA. What should the architect change?

opts.t: Apply fixed 512-token windows with 50-token overlap across every ticket thread instead.
Build a classifier that routes each message to whichever adjacent messages it depends on before embedding.
Re-chunk each thread as one whole-ticket chunk instead of one chunk per message, keeping the full exchange together.
Keep per-message chunking, and prepend the ticket's subject line to every message before embedding.

whyRight: A ticket's replies only make sense against the problem statement above them, so the ticket, not the message, is the unit that stands alone. Whole-thread chunks preserve that at any thread length up to 40 messages, without touching embedding size.

whyWrong.A: Fixed windows change how much text sits in a chunk, not where the boundary falls; a 512-token cut can still isolate a reply from its problem statement.
whyWrong.B: A dependency classifier is a new component with its own failure mode, built to solve a boundary problem that a per-ticket chunk already solves outright.
whyWrong.D: A subject line tells the model what the ticket is about but still leaves each reply's chunk missing the specific problem it was answering.

t1Clause: the knowledge base holds structured support threads of 3 to 40 messages
lessonKey: chunk message per ticket

stem: A field-service knowledge base mixes troubleshooting prose with inline part numbers, and 500 technicians query it using both plain descriptions and exact part numbers. Dense-only retrieval returns a 30% hit rate on part-number searches, a safety concern on critical equipment. What should the architect implement?

opts.t: Build a knowledge graph over the equipment hierarchy to resolve part-number lookups.
Replace dense retrieval with lexical-only search, since technicians mainly need exact part-number matches.
Keep dense-only retrieval, and have technicians manually check the part number in the parts catalog.
Add lexical retrieval alongside dense search and fuse the rankings for both query types.

whyRight: The corpus mixes prose and identifiers, and technicians query both ways, which is exactly the condition hybrid retrieval exists for. Fusing lexical and dense rankings recovers exact part-number matches without sacrificing the paraphrase tolerance plain-language descriptions still need.

whyWrong.A: A knowledge graph answers relationship questions like what superseded a part, not the exact-match problem a part-number search actually has here.
whyWrong.B: Technicians query both ways, by the scenario's own account; dropping dense retrieval would break every plain-language, paraphrased search that is not identifier-based.
whyWrong.C: Manual catalog lookup patches the miss after retrieval has already failed, and adds a step for every technician instead of fixing the search itself.

t1Clause: technicians query the corpus using both plain descriptions and exact part numbers
lessonKey: fused hybrid ranking

stem: A platform team must connect the agent to the organization's issue-tracking system used company-wide. An actively maintained community MCP server already exposes the equivalent operations, and a custom build needs three engineer-weeks requiring the engineering director's approval. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Build a custom MCP server duplicating the tracker's full API surface, spending the approved three-week budget.
Call the tracker directly from the orchestration layer on every request, bypassing model discretion.
Reject the community server as unreliable and commission a custom build, citing a lack of maintenance.
Adopt the actively maintained community MCP server instead of building a custom integration.

whyRight: A community MCP server already exposes the tracker's standard operations and is actively maintained, so custom effort should go where nothing else covers the workflow, without spending the approved budget or the director's time on infrastructure that already exists.

whyWrong.A: Building a custom server duplicates functionality an actively maintained community option already provides, spending scarce build budget on a solved problem this section reserves for genuinely unique workflows.
whyWrong.B: Direct orchestration-layer calls suit a mandatory step that must run on every request; connecting to a standard third-party system is a build-versus-adopt decision, not that one.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the server is actively maintained, which directly contradicts the claim of unreliable upkeep used to justify commissioning a custom build instead.

t1Clause: an actively maintained community MCP server already exposes the equivalent operations
lessonKey: community existing mcp server

stem: A production agent needs the same 4,000-token compliance policy block on every request, at 200,000 requests/day under a strict p95 latency SLA. An engineer proposes moving it into the progressive-discovery index so it loads only when needed. What should the architect decide?

opts.t: Move the block into the progressive-discovery index and fetch it with an extra model turn per request.
Expose it as a namespace-level index entry with on-demand expansion, matching the pattern for large tool surfaces.
Remove the block from the base prompt and rely on the model to request it only for compliance queries.
Keep the block ordered first in the base prompt, with prompt caching enabled.

whyRight: The block is required on every request, so nothing is actually being discovered; ordering it first and caching the prefix removes its latency cost without adding a round-trip that a fetch-on-demand design would introduce at this volume.

whyWrong.A: Fetching the block on demand adds a model turn to a request that always needs it, spending the round-trip cost this pattern exists to avoid.
whyWrong.B: Namespace indexing suits a large surface where most content is irrelevant to a given request; this block is required by every single request, so no expansion decision applies.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the block is needed on every request; skipping it and hoping the model asks for it risks compliance content being silently absent.

t1Clause: needs the same 4,000-token compliance policy block on every request
lessonKey: caching first order prompt

stem: An HR analytics tool queries a shared employee-records index through one internal service account for every request, and a manager should see only their own reports. Auditors require access decisions enforced and provable at query time. Select two corrections required.

opts.t: Propagate each requesting user's identity into the retrieval layer, replacing reliance on the shared service account alone.
Add a system-prompt instruction naming which tiers the agent may cite, leaving the shared account unchanged.
Apply the entitlement filter inside the retrieval query itself, before content is ranked or returned.
Replace the shared token with per-user credentials, though attribution to an outside operator was never required.

whyRight: The service account collapses every user into one identity at the point data is reached, so entitlement has to be re-established there: propagating the caller's identity and enforcing the filter inside the query are two separate, jointly required steps auditors can point to as proof.

whyWrong.B: A system-prompt rule is a probabilistic instruction the model might not follow; auditors need enforcement that is structurally deterministic, not asserted in a prompt.
whyWrong.D: Per-user credential substitution answers a third-party attribution requirement; this store is internal, so it adds credential-management overhead the situation does not call for.

t1Clause: internal service account

stem: A weekly invoice-reconciliation job processes 80,000 line items against a 2-hour runtime budget and keeps exceeding it. It waits for each complete model response before validating and posting to the ledger; an engineer proposes streaming to close the gap. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Enable streaming and report the improved time-to-first-token against the 2-hour runtime budget.
Reject streaming for this consumer and reduce total latency at the pipeline's slowest measured stage.
Enable streaming and report the run's improved mean per-item response time, while total weekly runtime still exceeds the 2-hour budget.
Add a monitoring alert that flags runtime-budget breaches after each weekly run, leaving the pipeline itself unchanged.

whyRight: The pipeline waits for each complete response before writing downstream, so time-to-first-token never mattered here; total latency is unchanged by streaming, and the SLA breach can only close by reducing time at the slowest measured stage.

whyWrong.A: Time-to-first-token only matters to a consumer reading incrementally; this pipeline waits for the complete response, so the reported metric never touches the 2-hour runtime budget it actually misses.
whyWrong.C: A mean per-item improvement can still leave the weekly run's total processing time over its 2-hour budget; streaming buys nothing for a consumer waiting on the full response before posting.
whyWrong.D: Flagging breaches after each weekly run confirms the budget was missed again; it does nothing to shorten the pipeline's slowest stage, which is what the miss is caused by.

t1Clause: parses each complete model response before writing downstream

stem: A team investigating an intermittent tool-call failure affecting under 1% of 500,000 daily requests proposes capturing full-fidelity traces for all traffic "temporarily, until the cause is found," though the data includes regulated customer records. What should the architect decide?

opts.t: Approve full-fidelity capture for two weeks across all traffic, then revert to the prior policy.
Take a small uniform sample of routine successes for a baseline, leaving error paths unsampled.
Log full request and response payloads for every trace, since this data is central to the diagnosis.
Reject full-fidelity capture; stratify at 100% for errors and low-confidence paths, with redacted metadata for regulated access.

whyRight: At this volume the failure is rare, so it needs its own 100% stratum rather than a slice of routine traffic; full-fidelity capture of everything is unaffordable here and duplicates regulated records into a second sensitive store.

whyWrong.A: A two-week window still captures full-fidelity traces of regulated records at this volume; deferring the cost and exposure decision does not remove either one.
whyWrong.B: A uniform sample of routine successes serves baseline detection, not diagnosing a rare failure; leaving error paths unsampled misses the exact events under investigation.
whyWrong.C: The stem states the data includes regulated customer records, which requires redacted payload at the point of access, not full unredacted request and response logging.

t1Clause: affecting under 1% of 500,000 daily requests
lessonKey: cost data exposure protection reject

stem: A policy-document RAG pipeline already contextualizes each chunk with its title and heading path before embedding, sized to answer multi-sentence questions. Finance wants chunk size cut further to reduce a rising embedding bill. What should the architect recommend?

opts.t: Shrink the chunk size as finance requests, since embedding cost scales directly with size.
Keep the current chunk size and contextualization, and reject the proposed further shrink.
Shrink the chunks but prepend an even longer heading path to compensate for the loss.
Fix the chunk boundaries to follow the document's structure instead of changing the size.

whyRight: The chunks are already sized correctly and contextualized for multi-sentence questions; shrinking further to cut cost would remove content those questions depend on. The stated requirement to retain enough surrounding context outranks an unstated cost target, so the current sizing stays.

whyWrong.A: Embedding cost does scale with size, but shrinking below what multi-sentence questions need breaks the stated context requirement to chase an unstated cost target.
whyWrong.C: A longer heading path adds context about structure, not the surrounding content a shrunken chunk just lost; the multi-sentence answer still is not there to retrieve.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the stem indicates the chunks are truncated or cut mid-idea; boundary structure is not the problem finance is asking to solve here.

t1Clause: to reduce a rising embedding bill
lessonKey: chunk contextualization current further keep proposed reject shrink size

stem: A team preparing to launch an assistant sets its content-safety target as a hard 0% policy-violation rate, graded by a model classifier over a rolling window of 10,000 conversations, ahead of trust-and-safety sign-off. What threshold should the team set?

opts.t: Keep the target at a literal 0% policy-violation rate and treat any single violation as a launch-blocking failure.
Enforce the 0% target with a deterministic pattern check against the model's raw output text.
Drop the numeric threshold and have the trust-and-safety lead review flagged conversations weekly instead.
Re-anchor the bar to a small achievable non-zero rate, such as under 0.1% of the sampled window.

whyRight: An open-ended, model-graded property cannot sustain a hard zero — one miss makes the bar non-binding and future violations go unflagged. Re-anchoring to a small, deliberately achievable non-zero rate, set before results are seen, keeps the threshold a real gate rather than an aspiration nobody enforces.

whyWrong.A: A literal 0% target on an open-ended, model-judged property becomes non-binding the first time any violation occurs, since the bar cannot be sustained.
whyWrong.B: The property is model-graded, not deterministic; no pattern or field scan can decide whether free-text output is policy-violating.
whyWrong.C: Removing the numeric threshold entirely leaves no gate at all, and weekly qualitative review cannot substitute for a measured, agreed-in-advance rate.

t1Clause: graded by a model classifier — invert to a deterministic exact-match scan for a specific forbidden token, making the property code-checkable
lessonKey: 0 000 1 10 anchor e g non rate re small zero

stem: A RAG assistant's single overall quality metric drops twelve points, and the team must isolate which layer caused it before the release manager will approve the next deploy. Applying the two-layer evaluation principle, what should the team do?

opts.t: Refine the rubric used to compute the single overall quality score.
Move the pipeline to a higher-capability generation model to raise the overall score.
Read the retrieval and generation bars already tracked separately, and treat retrieval as the likely fault.
Split the score into a retrieval row (Recall@k) and a generation row (faithfulness), each cleared against its own bar.

whyRight: A blended score cannot say which layer moved. Splitting into a retrieval row measured against gold passage ids and a generation row measured for faithfulness isolates the regression to the layer that actually failed, since each layer must clear its own bar independently.

whyWrong.A: A better rubric still scores one blended number, so it still cannot attribute a regression to retrieval or to generation specifically.
whyWrong.B: A higher-capability model was never shown to be at fault, and it can produce more fluent answers over the same broken passages.
whyWrong.C: The stem states there is only a single blended score; separate retrieval and generation bars do not yet exist to read.

t1Clause: one overall quality metric, regression cannot be located — invert to the retrieval and generation bars already being tracked separately at 0.55 and 0.97
lessonKey: generation into retrieval rows split

stem: A prompt change clears the regression set and a controlled A/B on pre-declared metrics with no guardrail breach, then ships in stages to 50,000 weekly tickets. A stakeholder later blames an unrelated production incident on 'that recent prompt change.' What should the team do?

opts.t: Roll back the prompt change immediately to satisfy the stakeholder, since it is the most recently shipped change.
Re-run the regression set and a new controlled A/B against the prompt change to confirm it is not the cause.
Do not roll back the change — regression and the A/B already cleared it; investigate the incident's real cause instead.
Escalate to a higher-capability model, since a production incident suggests the current model can no longer be trusted.

whyRight: The change already passed proper release testing — a regression evaluation and a controlled A/B that cleared its guardrails — so a coincidental timing complaint doesn't reopen it. Attribution now belongs to the actual production incident, which the validated change did not cause and rolling back would not fix.

whyWrong.A: Rolling back a change that already cleared regression and a controlled A/B discards validated evidence and treats timing coincidence as proof, without investigating the real cause.
whyWrong.B: The stem already states the change cleared its regression set and a controlled A/B; re-running the same tests re-investigates a variable the evidence already cleared.
whyWrong.D: Nothing in the evidence implicates the model, and a bigger model would not explain or fix a production incident the validated prompt change never caused.

t1Clause: the prompt change clears the regression set and a controlled A/B before rollout — invert so approval instead rests only on ten hand-picked examples that looked better, with no regression set or A/B ever run, making option B's overdue test the correct move
lessonKey: already b back cause change cleared do incident instead investigate real regression roll s

stem: An agent handles single-step lookups correctly but fails broadly on tasks needing three or more reasoning steps. Retrieval Recall@k is verified at 0.94 and the prompt has passed clean review. What does this pattern indicate before the team funds further prompt rewrites?

opts.t: Retrieval is still the likely fault, so Recall@k should be re-measured before any other conclusion is drawn.
The prompt still contains ambiguous wording and needs a further rewrite, despite passing review.
Model mismatch: the model's reasoning capability is insufficient for this task, since every upstream layer is already cleared.
The application is failing to resend conversation history, causing context loss across turns.

whyRight: Retrieval and prompt are the cheaper, earlier layers and both have already cleared, which is precisely the signature the diagnosis order reserves for model mismatch: a broad failure on genuinely multi-step reasoning after every upstream layer is confirmed clean.

whyWrong.A: The stem already states Recall@k is verified at 0.94, so retrieval has already cleared and cannot be the fault.
whyWrong.B: The prompt already passed clean review; another rewrite patches a layer that was never implicated in the failure.
whyWrong.D: Lost conversation history explains forgotten facts across turns, not a broad multi-step reasoning failure verified against clean retrieval and prompt.

t1Clause: The stem states Retrieval Recall@k 'is verified at 0.94'; invert to Recall@k has not yet been measured, which correctly justifies option A's 'should be re-measured before any conclusion is drawn.'

stem: A regulated support system sends an identical, compliance-mandated preamble on every request. Both p95 latency and monthly token cost exceed target, and the platform lead must approve the fix before next quarter's budget review. Select two appropriate actions.

opts.t: Cut the preamble by 60% to only the sections used most often.
Reorder the prompt so the static preamble comes first and enable prompt caching.
Add a model call at request time to summarize the preamble before sending it.
Decline the proposal to cut the preamble, since the removed sections are compliance-mandated.

whyRight: Reordering for a stable prefix and enabling caching reuses the same required content at a fraction of the cost and latency, while declining the cut preserves compliance-mandated sections a proposed 60% reduction would remove — both actions preserve everything the requirement demands.

whyWrong.A: Cutting the preamble removes compliance-mandated content to solve a problem caching solves without losing anything, and none of it may legally be dropped.
whyWrong.C: An extra model call sounds like a sophisticated compression step, but it adds its own full invocation cost and latency and degrades policy precision.

t1Clause: the preamble is compliance-mandated — invert so the removed sections are unrequired boilerplate rather than compliance content
lessonKey: caching content enable first if order prompt reject removed required sections static

stem: A document-classification pipeline processes 400,000 records weekly. The quality team reviews every customer complaint and every classifier-flagged output, but never samples outputs scored high-confidence. Which addition closes the monitoring gap?

opts.t: Add per-segment breakdowns to the existing weekly dashboard.
Raise the confidence classifier's threshold so fewer records qualify as high-confidence.
Add stratified sampling of the high-confidence stream, across segments and verdict classes.
Rely on the existing complaint and flagged-output reviews as sufficient coverage.

whyRight: The unsampled high-confidence stream is exactly where a novel error pattern first appears, since it never reaches a human through a complaint or a flag. Stratified sampling across segments and verdict classes gives the quality team visibility into that stream instead of waiting for a complaint.

whyWrong.A: Per-segment dashboard breakdowns fix aggregate masking on data already collected; they add nothing for records that were never sampled in the first place.
whyWrong.B: Narrowing the high-confidence label shrinks the unreviewed population without validating any of the records still inside it, leaving the same blind spot smaller but unmeasured.
whyWrong.D: The stem's own gap is that high-confidence records are never sampled, so complaints and flags cannot already cover error types that surface only in that unreviewed stream.

t1Clause: The stem states the pipeline 'never samples' the high-confidence stream; invert to 'already stratifies sampling across the high-confidence stream but the weekly dashboard reports only an aggregate average,' and per-segment breakdowns becomes the fix.
lessonKey: add confidence high sampling stratified stream

stem: A multi-tenant billing assistant must never state another customer's account identifier in a reply, and the compliance officer requires this metric defined before sign-off. Which threshold should the team set?

opts.t: A deterministic pattern or field scan enforced as a hard zero — 0 occurrences per N replies.
Re-anchor the bar to a small non-zero rate, such as fewer than 0.1% of 10,000 replies.
Calibrate the pass bar once a full month of baseline reply volume has been observed.
Log every reply and flag any that mention another customer's account number for review afterward.

whyRight: The requirement is exact and machine-checkable — a specific customer's account identifier either appears in the text or it does not. Code can enforce that boundary precisely, so the metric is a deterministic hard zero measured per N replies, not a rate description chosen after results arrive.

whyWrong.B: This re-anchoring move belongs to an open-ended, model-judged property; this requirement is exact and code-checkable, so a non-zero statistical rate weakens an enforceable boundary into a tolerance.
whyWrong.C: Waiting for baseline volume turns the bar into a description of whatever the system already does, and a deterministic property needs no baseline to define its threshold.
whyWrong.D: Flagging after emission only detects a violation that has already reached the customer; the requirement calls for a hard zero enforced before the reply ships, not a review queue afterward.

t1Clause: The requirement is deterministically checkable ('must never state another customer's account identifier'); invert to an open-ended, model-judged property (e.g., reply tone) proposed at a 0% bar, and re-anchoring to a small non-zero rate becomes the fix.
lessonKey: 0 check deterministic n per

stem: A coding assistant generates candidate functions behind a test harness that automatically reruns generation up to five times until the tests pass, before any code reaches a reviewer. Which aggregation should the engineering lead adopt to report reliability?

opts.t: `pass@k` — credit the harness for reachable success across the up-to-five attempts.
`pass^k` = 1.0 applied to every attempt, since each rerun is treated as customer-visible.
`pass^k`, since five attempts is a large enough sample to detect hidden instability.
Skip aggregation and rely on the reviewer, since every generated candidate already reaches human review.

whyRight: The test harness catches and reruns failing attempts before any output is exposed, so what matters is whether a passing candidate is reachable within the attempt budget. `pass@k` measures exactly that; the harness's own retries make individual-attempt reliability irrelevant to what the reviewer eventually sees.

whyWrong.B: Demanding a perfect first attempt across five retries ignores that the harness absorbs failures; this bar belongs to steps where a single silent failure reaches the world.
whyWrong.C: Attempt count measures how many times something was tried, not whether a failure is absorbed or exposed; that distinction, not the number five, decides the aggregation.
whyWrong.D: The stem places the harness before the reviewer stage, so only candidates that already passed the tests are ever seen; the reviewer never observes the failed attempts this option assumes.

t1Clause: The harness 'automatically reruns... before any code reaches a reviewer'; invert so every generated candidate deploys directly without passing through the harness, and pass^k becomes the correct aggregation.

stem: A contract-review assistant fabricates clause numbers only for contracts uploaded in the past week; older contracts are still handled correctly. The legal-ops lead wants this fixed before next week's compliance audit. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Move to a higher-capability model, since fabricated clause numbers signal a reasoning limitation.
Add an explicit system-prompt instruction not to state clause numbers it cannot verify.
Expand the evaluation set with more contract examples to measure the fabrication rate precisely.
Check how the newly uploaded contracts were chunked and indexed, since the failure is confined to that recent batch.

whyRight: The failure is confined to one recent batch of documents while everything else still works, which is the data-coverage and chunking signature, not a model deficiency. Checking how the new contracts were chunked and indexed tests the layer the symptom actually points to, before any model change is considered.

whyWrong.A: Fabrication confined to one recent batch is a data-layer signature, not a reasoning limitation; swapping models replaces a component the symptom never implicates.
whyWrong.B: An instruction not to overstate certainty treats the symptom, not the cause, and cannot conjure a clause number that was never correctly indexed in the first place.
whyWrong.C: A larger evaluation set would measure the fabrication rate more precisely without diagnosing which layer produces it, leaving the actual defect unaddressed before next week's audit.

t1Clause: The fabrication is 'confined to contracts uploaded in the past week'; invert to failure occurring broadly and uniformly with retrieval and chunking already verified clean, and moving to a higher-capability model becomes the fix.

stem: An agent pipeline has a p95 latency budget of 3 seconds and is currently averaging 4.1 seconds; no stage-level timing has been collected. Which action should the team take before changing anything?

opts.t: Enable prompt caching on the static portions of every request immediately.
Profile stage-level timing first to identify which stage dominates the overage.
Route routine requests to a smaller cascade model to cut generation time.
Reduce the retrieved passages sent to the model, since retrieval is clearly the slowest stage.

whyRight: Halving a stage that accounts for only a fraction of the total budget barely moves the aggregate number, so the first move is to measure which stage actually owns the 1.1-second overage. Every optimization lever below is real, but none of them is targeted until that measurement exists.

whyWrong.A: Caching is a real lever with no quality cost, but committing to it before profiling assumes the static preamble is the dominant stage, which the stem never establishes.
whyWrong.C: Cascade routing is a genuine lever elsewhere, but its trigger must be validated per segment; applying it before profiling assumes generation is the dominant stage without evidence.
whyWrong.D: The stem states no stage-level timing exists yet, which directly contradicts the claim that retrieval is clearly the slowest stage.

t1Clause: The stem states 'no stage-level timing has been collected'; invert to timing already showing the static preamble dominates the budget, and enabling prompt caching becomes the fix.

stem: A logistics-scheduling agent has kept an unused shipment-cancellation tool for six months. Ahead of the annual SOC 2 audit, the compliance lead's plan is to keep the tool active and log every invocation. What should replace this plan?

opts.t: Keep the tool active and route every invocation to a SIEM alert the compliance lead reviews before the audit.
Keep the tool, but require a supervisor's confirmation before each cancellation executes.
Remove the shipment-cancellation tool from the agent's toolset; six months of production use confirms the task never required it.
Route cancellation requests through a separate approval service that validates and executes them outside the agent's direct control.

whyRight: Six months of unused access with no legitimate need means the failure class can be eliminated rather than mitigated. Logging only records misuse after it happens; removing the tool takes away the capability a cancellation error would require, the strongest and cheapest control available here.

whyWrong.A: A SIEM alert only detects a cancellation after it executes; logging is appropriate when misuse is low-consequence and reversible, not for an unused, unassessed tool.
whyWrong.B: A supervisor's confirmation still leaves the tool and its capability in place, and the safeguard's strength depends entirely on how carefully that confirmation is given each time.
whyWrong.D: A separate approval service fits a tool still needed occasionally; this tool has gone unused six months, so the task needs no such capability at all.

t1Clause: kept an unused shipment-cancellation tool for six months
lessonKey: control primary reject

stem: A RAG assistant serving 5,000 daily support tickets began giving confident, incorrect answers this week. The knowledge corpus was reindexed Monday, and the model provider also rolled out a routine version update the same day. Select two correct first diagnostic steps.

opts.t: Investigate the retrieval pipeline — chunk boundaries, embedding version, and index freshness — for errors traceable to Monday's reindex.
Insert deterministic validation checkpoints between each step of the support pipeline to interrupt any compounding across steps.
Add an instruction to the system prompt directing the assistant to only answer from verified, high-confidence context.
Check the pinned model version against the prior release and run the regression set for the vendor's update.

whyRight: Two changes landed the same day, so both must be ruled in or out. The reindex timing points at the retrieval pipeline — chunking, embedding version, index freshness — while the concurrent vendor update requires checking the pinned model version and regression set before either cause is ruled out.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in the stem describes a multi-step chain where each step passes its own test yet the combined result is worse; that failure mode is not in evidence here.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction to only use verified context patches the model's output, not the two concurrent changes; it does nothing to check the reindex or the vendor's version update.

t1Clause: no multi-step chain is described where each step passes its own test yet the combined result is worse

stem: A bank's private-banking unit approves 15 wire transfers a month above $5 million, each requiring a compliance officer's sign-off. A digitization team proposes confidence-tiered auto-approval to modernize the process, auto-approving high-confidence transfers and routing only low-confidence ones to review. What should the team do?

opts.t: Adopt confidence-tiered auto-approval as proposed; it modernizes the workflow and still routes low-confidence transfers to review.
Keep full human review of every transfer regardless of confidence; volume is low, consequence is uniformly high.
Auto-approve all transfers above a set confidence score, and audit a sample of approvals each quarter.
Randomly sample 20% of transfers for compliance review each month, auto-approving the remainder.

whyRight: Fifteen high-dollar wire transfers a month is a volume a compliance team can review in full, and every transfer sits above the consequence threshold that requires a human regardless of confidence. Confidence-tiered auto-approval trades that certainty for throughput the volume never demanded in the first place.

whyWrong.A: Confidence-tiered routing is the right move at high volume with mixed consequence, but here every transfer is uniformly high-consequence — the confidence score has nothing to discount.
whyWrong.C: Removing routine review and relying on a quarterly sample abandons oversight on the very population — high-dollar transfers — the sign-off requirement exists to catch.
whyWrong.D: Sampling reviews transfers in proportion to how often they occur, not their consequence, so a costly transfer is no more likely to be the one reviewed.

t1Clause: approves 15 wire transfers a month
lessonKey: correct every human item review

stem: A payments platform tokenizes cardholder data before it leaves the cardholder-data environment, so downstream services only see tokens. A case-management team investigating a disputed charge needs the real name behind one specific token, for a documented, narrow reason. What should the team add?

opts.t: Re-associate the record's identity locally using the map already held inside the boundary, and log the access.
Let the case-management team query the cardholder-data environment directly for this investigation, bypassing the tokenization layer.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to disclose the real name only for documented case-management requests.
Commission a compliance review of the entire tokenization architecture before allowing any re-identification for this case.

whyRight: The boundary already tokenizes correctly, so a narrow, documented need for a specific record's real identity is answered inside that same design: re-associate locally using the identity map the boundary already holds, and log the access. Nothing about a legitimate use case licenses loosening the boundary itself.

whyWrong.B: Bypassing tokenization for this workflow reopens the exposure the boundary exists to prevent; a narrow legitimate need calls for local re-association, not for lifting the boundary.
whyWrong.C: A prompt instruction is evaluated after the model already holds the real identity, and fits a preference, not this absolute boundary requirement.
whyWrong.D: A full architecture review answers a broader question than this request and delays a narrow, already-scoped need without changing whether the tokenization boundary itself is sound.

t1Clause: tokenizes cardholder data before it leaves the cardholder-data environment
lessonKey: access already associate boundary held identity inside locally log map re record s using

stem: To meet a compliance deadline without building new logging, an audit lead proposes having the model generate a short explanation attached to every declined application, to serve as the audit record for regulators. What is the correct next step?

opts.t: Provide the generated explanation to declined applicants for their own understanding, and file it as the audit record too.
Keep the generated explanation as the audit record, and add a disclaimer noting it may not be fully accurate.
Commission an independent model audit to certify the explanation generator's overall reliability before regulators review any decisions.
Remove the generated explanation as the audit record, and log the inputs, evidence, versions, and threshold behind each decision.

whyRight: A generated rationale is confidently wrong about its own causes exactly when it matters most, so it cannot serve as evidence of what happened. Removing it from the audit role and logging the inputs, evidence, versions, and threshold that actually produced each decision reconstructs the real path regulators need.

whyWrong.A: Handing the explanation to applicants is fine, but filing that same generated text as the regulator's audit record is what the section rules out.
whyWrong.B: A disclaimer describes the record's limits without changing what it is; the audit still rests on text produced after the fact, not a trace of what happened.
whyWrong.C: Certifying the generator's general reliability answers a different question than what determined this specific decision, and the compliance deadline does not allow time for an independent audit anyway.

t1Clause: to serve as the audit record for regulators
lessonKey: audit end record useful user

stem: An internal reporting agent holds a tool that can permanently delete customer records, though its stated task is read-only summarization. The security lead added invocation logging and asks whether that satisfies the least-privilege requirement before sign-off.

opts.t: Confirm the existing invocation logging and monthly audit review satisfy the least-privilege requirement.
Require a second engineer's sign-off before each delete-tool invocation executes.
Move the delete tool to a scoped service account with tighter database permissions and continuous monitoring.
Remove the delete tool from the agent's tool definitions, since the task does not need it.

whyRight: Least privilege is satisfied by removing a capability the task does not need, not by monitoring its use. Deleting the delete tool eliminates the failure class entirely, while logging, sign-off, and scoped permissions only detect or narrow a capability that should not exist.

whyWrong.A: Logging and periodic audit review record misuse after it happens; they do not stop the deletion from executing, which is the audit misconception this section corrects.
whyWrong.B: A second-engineer sign-off is a partial gate that still leaves the delete capability available and depends on whoever grants the approval.
whyWrong.C: A scoped service account and tighter permissions still preserve a delete capability the task never required; thorough permissioning is not the same as removing it.

t1Clause: holds a tool that can permanently delete customer records, though its stated task is read-only summarization

stem: Finance requires that every extracted payment amount match its source invoice before an assistant approves 12,000 monthly payments, and asks which verification step reliably catches figures the model transcribed incorrectly.

opts.t: Have the same model re-read the invoice and re-confirm the extracted figure without external comparison.
Compare every extracted figure against the invoice's original structured field before the payment posts.
Route the extraction through a second, independently trained model and post only when both agree.
Manually verify a random five percent sample of approved payments each week for accuracy.

whyRight: Comparing every extracted figure against the invoice's own structured field is a deterministic check that fails independently of the model's generation process, matching the section's rule that only a check drawn from outside the model reliably catches confident, incorrect figures.

whyWrong.A: A second read by the same model shares its generation process and failure mode; asking a model to re-check itself is not independent verification.
whyWrong.C: Two independently trained models can still share correlated training data and agree while both are wrong, so agreement is not equivalent to independent evidence.
whyWrong.D: Finance requires every figure caught before approval; a weekly five-percent sample lets most mismatches post before anyone reviews them.

t1Clause: every extracted payment amount match its source invoice
lessonKey: against comparison deterministic source structured

stem: A federal agency's FedRAMP authorization confines every workload to its approved environment. A project drafting marketing copy from public press releases, touching no protected data, faces a six-week queue to enter that environment, and the program office asks how to proceed.

opts.t: Grant a scoped, reviewed exception for this specific low-risk workload, leaving the general authorized-environment requirement intact.
Relax the authorized-environment requirement generally so future public-data workloads can bypass the queue without individual review.
Require the marketing project to wait in the standard authorization queue like every other workload, regardless of content.
Let the model classify each output as public or sensitive, routing sensitive content to the authorized environment.

whyRight: FedRAMP authorization is a property of the environment itself, not something an individual workload can be exempted around. Waiting in the standard queue routes this project through the authorized environment exactly like every other workload — the compliance path section 5.4 actually describes, not a scoped exception that was never part of the mechanism.

whyWrong.A: A scoped exception sounds like a proportionate, risk-based compromise, but authorization is a property of the environment; no exception process, however narrow, confers it on a workload that has not gone through the authorized path.
