whyWrong.B: Relaxing the requirement generally reopens the boundary for future workloads that may not stay public, undoing the protection the authorization exists to provide.
whyWrong.D: A model-side classifier is probabilistic; whenever it misclassifies, content would bypass the authorized environment the requirement exists to enforce.

t1Clause: confines every workload to its approved environment
lessonKey: authorised data environment keep model out route through unavailable

stem: A hiring-screening model cannot equalize its selection rate and false-negative rate across two demographic groups because their base rates differ. The model risk committee, already using a stratified equal-N sample, must decide how to proceed before the next audit.

opts.t: Escalate to legal counsel without specifying which fairness definition will govern the model going forward.
Continue retraining until both parity constraints are satisfied at the same threshold.
Decide which harm the model must avoid, select the matching fairness definition, and document the rationale.
Rebalance the evaluation sample to equal N per group, since the smaller group's sample size is driving the conflict.

whyRight: Equal selection rate and equal false-negative rate cannot both hold when base rates differ, so the resolution is a stated choice: name the harm being controlled, select the fairness definition that controls it, and record the rationale for the audit trail.

whyWrong.A: Escalating without naming a fairness definition leaves the conflict unresolved and produces no documented rationale for the audit.
whyWrong.B: Base rates already differ, so retraining toward both parity constraints at once chases a target the section says cannot generally be reached.
whyWrong.D: The sample is already stratified with equal N per group, so rebalancing again does not address why the two metrics conflict; base rates differ instead.

t1Clause: already using a stratified equal-N sample
lessonKey: being choose controlled harm rationale record which

stem: A compliance team requires that every AI-flagged transaction above a risk threshold pass through a two-person sequential review, the second reviewer blind to the first, under a documented regulatory audit expectation. How should the architect handle this review workflow?

opts.t: Continue eliciting the cost of a missed versus falsely flagged transaction, since that determines the review workflow design.
Implement the two-person sequential blind review exactly as specified; it is a non-negotiable attestation requirement, not an optimization suggestion.
Propose a confidence-weighted single-reviewer model that the architect judges more efficient, then present it as an improvement to the sponsor.
Escalate to the sponsor's leadership that the two-step sequential requirement is unnecessarily slow and should be reconsidered before build starts.

whyRight: The two-person sequential blind review is how each flagged decision's accountability is verified, under a documented regulatory audit expectation — an external attestation requirement, not a design preference the architect can trade away. However sound the engineering, a redesign that removes or reshapes that verification step is out of scope; the architect implements it exactly as specified.

whyWrong.A: The workflow is already fixed by a named regulatory audit expectation; treating it as still open to a cost-of-error elicitation misreads an external attestation requirement as an unbounded design question.
whyWrong.C: Replacing the mandated two-person blind review with a more efficient single-reviewer design substitutes the architect's engineering preference for a constraint that is external and not tradeable against efficiency gains.
whyWrong.D: The two-person sequential review is the attestation the regulator requires, not a build-schedule inconvenience; framing it as negotiable misreads an external, non-negotiable constraint as an internal scheduling preference.

t1Clause: under a documented regulatory audit expectation
lessonKey: blind compliance driven exactly implement implementation optimize person requirement review sequential specified suggestion two

stem: A sponsor's risk committee has mandated that this system's monthly governance report show the end-to-end error rate after human review, computed against the full production population, per the committee's charter. How should the architect handle this month's report?

opts.t: Report accuracy broken out by document type with the end-to-end outcome, since segmentation is generally the more informative reporting practice.
Decline to finalize this month's report until the committee agrees to add per-segment breakdowns alongside the mandated figure.
Produce the end-to-end error rate after human review exactly as specified; the mandated metric and cadence are the governance requirement.
Propose adding a composite risk score the architect judges more informative, alongside the committee's requested figure.

whyRight: The committee's charter names the exact metric and cadence, so that mechanism is the governance requirement itself, not the sponsor's rough idea of what a report should contain. A more segmented or additional metric, however useful, is out of scope for this deliverable.

whyWrong.A: Segmentation is the right move only when no specific metric has been mandated; here it substitutes the architect's own report design for a chartered requirement.
whyWrong.B: Withholding the mandated report over a preferred addition treats a governance requirement as negotiable, delaying a deliverable the committee is entitled to on schedule.
whyWrong.D: Adding a metric nobody chartered is a more elaborate report than requested, not a compliant one; the committee asked for one specific figure.

t1Clause: per the committee's charter
lessonKey: after cadence end error exactly governance human mandated metric produce rate requirement review specified

stem: A team's structured correction loop captures input, output, expected output, and reviewer for every fix in a document-extraction pipeline. A sponsor cites one thoroughly documented correction as proof the underlying issue is now fixed and won't recur. What should the architect do?

opts.t: Accept the documented correction as proof the issue is resolved, since the structured loop confirms it was captured correctly.
Check the accumulated evaluation set for whether this failure mode recurs across cases before crediting the fix.
Establish a new recurring review reporting real production performance against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Tell the sponsor no correction can be credited without a controlled experiment isolating the cause.

whyRight: The structured loop is correctly capturing input, output, expected output, and reviewer for each correction; that record is what determines whether a failure recurs. One documented correction, however thorough, is a single case — check the accumulated evaluation set for a recurrence pattern before crediting the fix.

whyWrong.A: A well-captured single case confirms the loop is working, not that the failure won't recur; recurrence is read from the accumulated record, not one entry.
whyWrong.C: The structured loop already exists and is functioning; the gap is reading one entry as proof, not a missing recurring mechanism to build.
whyWrong.D: The existing structured record can already settle recurrence without a new experiment; refusing to read it abandons evidence the loop already provides.

t1Clause: captures input, output, expected output, and reviewer for every fix
lessonKey: accumulated across before cases check crediting evaluation failure fix mode recurs set whether

stem: A chunking-strategy choice made to fit a small context-window limit a year ago is now moot after a context-window upgrade. The only surviving design record is a slide summarizing the final approach. What should the architect have recorded to make that original decision reopenable?

opts.t: Record the decision, the rejected alternatives with their numbers, the trade-off accepted, and the context-window limit that drove the choice.
Check the recorded constraint and re-evaluate the decision now that the ceiling has changed.
Produce a comprehensive written description of the current architecture with detailed component diagrams for the receiving team.
Hold another recorded walkthrough covering the new context-window limit and how it affects the design.

whyRight: A decision record needs the decision, the rejected alternatives with their numbers, the trade-off accepted, and the constraint that drove the choice; only that lets the team check the ceiling change against the original reasoning and reopen the decision on evidence.

whyWrong.B: No constraint was ever recorded here, only a slide was kept, so there is nothing written to check against the new context-window limit.
whyWrong.C: A thorough description of the current design, however detailed, carries no reasoning; it cannot show whether the relaxed ceiling changes the original trade-off.
whyWrong.D: A second walkthrough transfers understanding once more to whoever attends, but leaves no written record the next reviewer can check against a future change.

t1Clause: the only surviving design record is a slide summarizing the final approach

stem: An automated invoice-triage tool ran cleanly across a 3-branch trial, misrouting one invoice in every 350 twice during the trial while staff caught and hand-corrected 15% of routed invoices. Leadership wants it rolled out to all 45 branches. Select two actions to take first.

opts.t: Treat the observed failure rate and review proportion as fixed percentages that hold unchanged at higher volume.
Plan for the 1-in-350 failure as a routine event at the new volume, not as a rare edge case.
Convert the 15% review proportion observed in the pilot into a staffing line sized to the projected rollout volume.
Size infrastructure capacity and rate limits for the new volume, and treat that as the binding constraint on readiness.

whyRight: A failure recurring twice during a 3-branch trial is frequent at fifteen times the volume across 45 branches, so it must be planned as routine, not rare. The 15% review load actually measured in the trial is the only sound basis for staffing the wider rollout.

whyWrong.A: The observed rates are exactly what must be re-examined at the new scale, not treated as fixed; freezing them skips the assumption audit that scaling requires.
whyWrong.D: Infrastructure and rate-limit sizing is real and necessary, but it is not the binding constraint here; the failure rate and review load are what actually bite at this scale.

t1Clause: staff hand-corrected 15% of routed invoices
lessonKey: before convert event line plan projected rollout routine staffing volume

stem: A fraud-review sponsor has set a 92% precision target on flagged transactions, a monthly held-out evaluation set stratified by channel, and priced a false decline at $40 against a missed case at $600. What should the architect do next?

opts.t: Continue eliciting until the sponsor can state what an error costs, before moving to design.
Escalate to the sponsor's leadership that the requirement remains too underspecified to design against.
Select the highest-capability model and add a second independently sourced evaluation set before finalising design.
Proceed to design using the stated target, measurement method, evaluation set, and priced error costs.

whyRight: All four requirement parts — target, measurement method, evaluation set, and priced error cost — are already stated and stratified to the real channel mix; nothing about the requirement remains unbounded, so the architect should move directly into design.

whyWrong.A: The sponsor already priced both error directions ($40 versus $600); asking them to state what an error costs treats already-given information as still missing.
whyWrong.B: The requirement is already bounded and priced; escalating it as unactionable misstates the situation and stalls a decision the architect is equipped to make now.
whyWrong.C: Capability and a second evaluation set are unpriced additions the stated requirement never asked for; the precision target and existing set are already sufficient to design against.

t1Clause: the sponsor has already priced a false decline at $40 against a missed case at $600

stem: A hospital operations director asks during a quarterly review why nurses, who are legally accountable for the care summaries they sign, still countersign 20% of AI-drafted output at 97% model accuracy. How should the architect respond?

opts.t: Identify which countersigned decisions carry legal accountability or resist ground-truth checks, and state each one's automation risk.
Explain that AI systems are inherently probabilistic, and human oversight is standard safety practice at this accuracy level.
Commit in writing to removing the nurse countersignature step entirely once quarterly model accuracy exceeds 99%.
State that the countersignature is a legacy workflow step no longer necessary at current accuracy, and schedule its removal.

whyRight: The useful answer names which specific decisions carry accountability a person must attest to, or that the system cannot verify against ground truth, and states the risk of automating each — a generic appeal to model imperfection gives the director nothing to act on.

whyWrong.B: True but unspecific: restating that AI is probabilistic does not tell the director which decisions could be automated and which cannot, or what each risks.
whyWrong.C: Promises a future guarantee on decisions whose obstacle is legal accountability, not accuracy; higher accuracy never removes the need for someone to attest to the outcome.
whyWrong.D: Treats a legally accountable step as a removable technicality; the countersignature exists because someone must attest to the outcome, not because a workflow is unfinished.

t1Clause: nurses, who are legally accountable for the care summaries they sign

stem: A CFO deciding whether to renew a document-classification contract asks for the complete metrics dashboard — accuracy, latency percentiles, per-token cost, and override rates — attached to the renewal memo so nothing is missed. What should the architect report?

opts.t: Attach the complete dashboard export as requested, since more data supports a fuller renewal decision.
Report per-segment accuracy, latency percentiles, and the failure taxonomy for the current model version.
Report cost per processed item and its trajectory at the renewal volume, and state plainly that this figure excludes accuracy.
Wait until quarter-end actuals arrive before reporting any renewal metric, to avoid a partial picture.

whyRight: The CFO's decision is renewal economics, so cost per item and its trend at the volume the contract will actually run at is the metric that informs it; naming that it excludes accuracy keeps the CFO from over-reading it.

whyWrong.A: More metrics is not a fuller picture; it hands the CFO an unfiltered export and the interpretation job the architect is positioned to do.
whyWrong.B: Per-segment accuracy, latency, and failure taxonomy are real engineering-tuning metrics; they answer a retuning decision, not the renewal economics the CFO is deciding.
whyWrong.D: Delays the interpretation the CFO's decision needs now, and quarter-end actuals do not change which metric answers a renewal question.

t1Clause: a CFO deciding whether to renew

stem: Fourteen months after a model-tier decision shipped under an 800ms latency ceiling, the ceiling relaxes to 1500ms. The surviving record is a narrative description with diagrams; no original evaluator remains. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Check the constraint recorded in the original decision record, and re-evaluate the model tier against the new ceiling.
Commission a more comprehensive architecture description and updated component diagrams of the current pipeline.
Treat the choice as unrecorded in reopenable form, and reconstruct the alternatives, trade-offs, and constraint it originally rested on.
Leave the current model tier in place and monitor cost and latency telemetry, revisiting only if it degrades.

whyRight: The narrative and diagrams describe what was built, not why; with no evaluator left to ask, the decision cannot be reopened until the alternatives, trade-offs, and the constraint that drove it are reconstructed and checked against the new ceiling.

whyWrong.A: No constraint was ever recorded — only a narrative and diagrams survive — so there is nothing on file to check against the new ceiling.
whyWrong.B: A more comprehensive description of the current system adds pages, not the reasoning; it still cannot tell the team whether the choice still holds.
whyWrong.D: Monitoring telemetry detects a failure after it happens; a ceiling change is a known trigger to re-evaluate the decision now, not a reason to wait for degradation.

t1Clause: the surviving record is a narrative description with diagrams (no constraint was recorded)

stem: A supply-chain team's skill was recently broadened to scan supplier price feeds, and now invokes a live stock-adjustment command that should never fire without a controller's sign-off; the model version is unchanged. The scan also floods context before the 2-hour finance-close deadline. Select two fixes.

opts.t: Scope `allowed-tools` in the skill's frontmatter to exclude the stock-adjustment command.
Set `context: fork` for the price-feed scan so only its summary returns to the main conversation.
Add a project-wide `deny` rule in `settings.json` blocking the stock-adjustment command for every skill and integration.
Pin the model version, since a version change most likely caused the skill to start invoking the command.

whyRight: Two independent gaps exist: the skill's own tool access was never scoped, so `allowed-tools` must exclude the stock-adjustment command, and its price-feed scan pollutes the same context the deadline depends on, which `context: fork` isolates without touching the tool boundary.

whyWrong.C: Blocking the command project-wide affects every other skill and integration too; the sign-off gap belongs to this one skill's own tool access, not to a company-wide restriction.
whyWrong.D: The model version is stated as unchanged, so drift cannot explain why the command started firing; the cause is a tool boundary the frontmatter never set.

t1Clause: should never fire without a controller's sign-off (restricted to this one skill only)
lessonKey: allowed context fork frontmatter s scope set skill tools

stem: A finance-ops team's nightly reconciliation job runs unattended in a cron container, fetches related ledger entries mid-analysis to confirm each anomaly, and feeds a pipeline that pages on-call by severity. One malformed record broke a night's paging. Which mechanism fits the requirement?

opts.t: Add `-p` (`--print`) so the job runs non-interactively instead of waiting on stdin.
Run with `--output-format json` and enforce `--json-schema` so every finding carries a guaranteed, parseable shape.
Move the job to the Batch API, since nobody is waiting and it costs half as much.
Add a detailed 'Output Format' section to the project's CLAUDE.md describing the exact JSON shape every finding must follow.

whyRight: `--output-format json` combined with `--json-schema` guarantees every finding carries a well-formed, parseable shape on every run, which the downstream pipeline's severity-based paging depends on; a nightly cron schedule and a mid-analysis ledger lookup do not change that requirement.

whyWrong.A: Running non-interactively stops the job from hanging on stdin, but says nothing about whether each finding's fields are well-formed enough for the pipeline to parse.
whyWrong.C: The job fetches related ledger entries mid-analysis, and the Batch API cannot execute a tool mid-request and return the result, disqualifying it regardless of the flexible deadline.
whyWrong.D: A CLAUDE.md description raises the odds of a well-formed record but never guarantees one; the parser still fails on the first run that deviates from the description.

t1Clause: The stem states the job 'feeds a pipeline that pages on-call by severity' and 'One malformed record broke a night's paging' — the evidence that forces a guaranteed schema. Invert by deleting that consumer and the malformed-record evidence entirely, leaving only 'runs unattended in a cron container' as the operative fact, which correctly justifies option A's non-interactive `-p` fix instead.
lessonKey: format json output schema

stem: A clinical-operations agent's configuration must guarantee patient identifiers never leave the de-identified pipeline no matter how a request is phrased, and that every export attempt is captured in the compliance audit trail. Select two settings changes that guarantee this.

opts.t: Add a strongly-worded instruction to the project CLAUDE.md forbidding identifier exports and reminding the agent to log every export.
Escalate both rules to managed enterprise policy settings, even though only this one agent's configuration is affected.
Add a `deny` rule for the identifier-export command pattern to `settings.json` permissions.
Add a hook, scoped to export events by `matcher`, that writes the audit-log entry automatically.

whyRight: A `deny` rule blocks the export outside model discretion regardless of prompt wording, and a hook scoped to export events writes the audit-log entry every time one fires — both are enforced by Claude Code itself, independent of what any instruction asks the agent to do.

whyWrong.A: A CLAUDE.md instruction shapes what the agent tries to do; it does not change what Claude Code allows, so a determined or malformed prompt can still trigger the export.
whyWrong.B: Managed policy fits a rule that must survive every local override across many machines; escalating one agent's rule there is more governance than a single agent's configuration needs.

t1Clause: The stem scopes the requirement to 'a clinical-operations agent's configuration' — one agent's own settings.json. Invert by making it a rule that must hold across every developer machine and survive local overrides, which correctly justifies option B's managed-policy escalation instead of a single agent's settings.json deny.
lessonKey: deny event hook json matcher permissions relevant rule scoped settings

stem: A twelve-engineer team's masking convention has always reached everyone. This week a new engineer's code omits it, the same day a teammate merges an unrelated rules file. The other eleven still see it; root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged. What should the team check first?

opts.t: Revert the unrelated rules-file merge, since it landed the same day the symptom appeared.
Run `/context` in the new engineer's session, since the convention may live only in the other engineers' personal configuration.
Have the new engineer restate the convention in every prompt until someone fixes it properly.
Post the convention in the onboarding channel and link it from the new-hire welcome email.

whyRight: The masking convention has always reached everyone, so the coincidental same-day rules-file merge is not the cause; root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged, meaning the convention was never centralized there. `/context` shows what the new engineer's session actually loaded, confirming whether it is missing entirely.

whyWrong.A: Reverting the merge treats same-day timing as causal, but root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged and the merge scopes an unrelated rule — the coincidence explains nothing.
whyWrong.C: Restating the convention per prompt patches each session downstream of a configuration gap `/context` would locate, and fails silently the moment someone forgets.
whyWrong.D: Posting to a channel transfers the knowledge to a human, not to the model's own request, and does not explain why only the new engineer lacks it.

t1Clause: The stem pins 'root `CLAUDE.md` is unchanged' to rule out the coincidental merge. Invert by removing that pinned fact, which reopens the same-day merge as a live suspect and correctly justifies option A's revert instead.
lessonKey: configuration context convention engineer engineers live may new only other personal run s session since
